strengths: The paper identifies a plausible failure mode in LLM-based architecture editing—single rewrites coupling operator definitions, action-level wiring, and interfaces—and proposes an intuitive factor-local editing mechanism using explicit routing, tagged code regions, and feasibility checks.

The controlled comparison against OpenEvolve attempts to hold the evolutionary backbone and base LLM fixed. The paper also reports useful diagnostics beyond final accuracy, including proposal validity, diff-based entanglement, best-so-far progress, MACs, and module ablations.

The discovered DFS architecture transfers without task-specific search to many other CLRS tasks and produces substantial improvements on several of them, including DFS, strongly connected components, sorting, and optimal BST. The full 30-task table also honestly exposes important negative-transfer cases.

The manuscript is generally organized and visually readable, provides pseudocode and selected architecture listings, includes an impact statement, and distinguishes proposal attempts from fully evaluated candidates. weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is internally inconsistent. The text says the 83.74% DFS architecture is found at proposal attempt 57, “corresponding to 57 evaluated candidates,” but Figure 2c shows SPARK's cumulative valid rate near 0.5 around that point. Under the paper's own definition—failed proposals do not enter evaluation—attempt 57 cannot simultaneously be evaluation 57. This directly undermines the claimed 28.1× evaluation-efficiency figure.

The headline 83.74% result appears to be a selected trajectory without uncertainty. Figure A.1 is described as a five-seed DFS search analysis, yet its seed curves finish around 0.22–0.25 OOD accuracy rather than near 0.837. The paper neither reconciles this discrepancy nor reports per-seed final scores, mean/standard deviation, confidence intervals, or statistical tests for the main table. Consequently, it is unclear whether the main result is representative or a lucky run.

The “28.1× speedup” is not established by a matched sample-efficiency experiment. It divides EvoPrompting's published 1600-evaluation budget by SPARK's claimed 57 evaluations even though EvoPrompting never attains SPARK's target accuracy and uses a different search setup. This is an endpoint ratio, not time-to-threshold or an efficiency curve under controlled LLM, backbone, proposal, and evaluation budgets. SPARK also uses multiple role-specific LLM calls and rejection filtering, but token, API, wall-clock, and preprocessing costs are not compared.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed causal mechanism. “ASR only” and “RC+SAR only” are insufficiently specified, and there are no controls for random or fixed factor selection, region-constrained editing without learned routing, feasibility filtering alone, or equal numbers of LLM calls. Thus the gain could arise from manually restricting the search space, additional prompting/inference, or rejection checks rather than progressive knowledge activation specifically.

Reporting is contradictory and selectively emphasizes favorable tasks. The main table contains ten tasks on which SPARK wins, while Table A.1 contains 30 tasks and shows severe regressions such as BFS (100.0 for EvoPrompting versus 70.6) and Floyd–Warshall (61.4 versus 32.9). Nevertheless, the conclusion states improvements on 12/18 tasks and superiority to EvoPrompting on 10/18, inconsistent with both the stated 30-task appendix and the displayed values. The text also elsewhere calls the supplement an 18-task evaluation.

The scope is narrow relative to the broad NAS framing: one manually partitioned component of the CLRS reference architecture is searched on one task, using two hand-defined disjoint regions, and the resulting architecture is transferred. There is no image, language, or broader NAS benchmark and no architecture whose factors are not naturally separable. The idea is useful but resembles established structured mutation and constrained code editing; the manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate backbone-agnostic applicability or strong conceptual originality beyond this instantiation.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The promised exact region definitions, complete evolution traces, and implementation details are not actually supplied; neither are the role prompts, sanitization rules, archive discretization, migration period, retry limits, cascade procedure, CLRS training hyperparameters, random seeds, checkpoint-selection protocol, or runnable code. Claims such as “default OpenEvolve settings” and “standard CLRS protocol” do not uniquely specify the experiment, especially for newly adapted baselines.

The entanglement analysis is partly tautological: SPARK explicitly rejects edits outside the selected tagged region, while entanglement is defined as touching multiple regions or frozen scaffolding. A lower measured entanglement rate therefore follows by construction. Evidence is needed that factor isolation—not merely filtering invalid proposals—improves performance at matched numbers of valid evaluations and matched LLM cost.

Presentation overstates what the evidence supports. Claims of “algorithmic alignment,” reliable activation of knowledge, and attribution of gains to reduced interference are not demonstrated mechanistically; the evidence is correlational. The impact discussion is acceptable for this low-risk benchmark study but cursory about substantial LLM/NAS compute and dependence on a proprietary API endpoint. Overall, the promising idea is outweighed by material inconsistencies in the central efficiency and robustness claims.

strengths: The motivation is understandable: explicitly scoping LLM code edits could improve validity and credit assignment during iterative NAS.
The method attempts a precise operationalization using region tags, factor-local diffs, feasibility checks, and separate accounting of proposals and trained evaluations.
The evaluation considers MACs, two LLM editors, cross-task transfer, and search-dynamics diagnostics.
The work presents no apparent material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The evolution listings contradict the central factor-locality constraint. Iterations 1, 2, 46, and 57 describe simultaneous Operator and Action changes even though Eq. 4 requires the non-selected region to remain byte-identical. Iteration 46 also changes the `_compute_tri_msgs` signature despite the claimed frozen-interface invariant. It is therefore unclear whether the reported search implemented SPARK as specified.

The headline 28.1x efficiency claim is unsupported. It compares EvoPrompting's 1600 evaluations from a different regime with one SPARK run. The claim that proposal attempt 57 corresponds to 57 evaluated candidates also conflicts with Figure 2c, where SPARK's cumulative valid rate drops well below one; under the stated accounting, many attempted proposals were not evaluated.

The empirical record is internally inconsistent. The main text and conclusion refer to 18 CLRS tasks, while Table A.1 contains 30. Figure A.1 reports five-seed best-so-far accuracy around 0.22–0.25, which is irreconcilable with the claimed 83.74% DFS result and Figure 2 unless an unexplained different metric is being plotted.

The causal evidence is insufficient. SPARK's lower cross-region entanglement is largely guaranteed by its rejection rule. The experiments do not adequately separate the effects of region enforcement, feasibility filtering, extra routing/directive calls, and the search backbone. The ASR-only and RC+SAR-only variants are not defined well enough to interpret.

Comparisons are not consistently controlled. SPARK uses three LLM calls per proposal, but the proposal budget ignores this additional inference cost. EvoPrompting is compared using a different search setting, while the adaptations of FunSearch, EoH, and OpenEvolve lack enough detail to verify their fidelity. Most results are point estimates without uncertainty or statistical tests.

Reproducibility is inadequate: prompts, full tagged templates, archive discretization, sanitization, training hyperparameters, per-seed results, baseline adaptations, and executable code are absent. The claimed complete traces are not present; only selected snapshots are supplied. Unspecified OpenEvolve defaults and a black-box API add further ambiguity.

Originality and significance are limited. The method is essentially manually engineered two-region constrained code editing, related to established structured editing and mutation operators. Search is performed only on DFS in one CLRS architecture family, leaving claims of backbone-agnostic and generally reliable LLM-driven NAS unsupported.

The paper selectively emphasizes a favorable 10-task subset despite substantial appendix regressions such as BFS and Floyd–Warshall. Speculative explanations of evolved components are presented without validating the claimed mechanisms. The central contradictions and irreconcilable accounting make the results unreliable enough to warrant strong rejection.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3abe9431ed784d6e821621fe140a5e60/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} identifies a concrete and important failure mode in LLM-driven NAS: free-form edits can couple operator definitions, forward-pass wiring, and interface constraints. Making the intervention scope explicit is sensible and practically useful.

SPARK is presented clearly as a composition of scope routing, directive generation, scoped refinement, and inexpensive feasibility checks. The region-based locality criterion is operationally defined, and the algorithms are easy to follow.

The reported empirical gains are potentially significant. The selected 10-task results show 83.92% mean OOD accuracy versus 79.43% for the strongest listed baseline, while MACs remain close to the CLRS reference. The full 30-task appendix also exposes important negative-transfer cases rather than reporting only successes.

The ASR/RC+SAR ablation is directionally informative: both components help under two LLM editors, and their combination gives the strongest DFS result without materially increasing MACs. Testing both DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus provides some evidence that the effect is not tied to one editor.
The paper is visually polished and generally readable. The impact statement is brief but adequate for this relatively low-risk methodological work, and I see no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central 28.1x efficiency claim is not supported by internally consistent accounting. The paper says the best result occurs at proposal attempt 57, "corresponding to 57 evaluated candidates," but Figure 2c shows a cumulative valid rate of only about 0.5 at that point; under the paper's own definition, this implies roughly 28-30 evaluated candidates, not 57. Moreover, comparing only full evaluations ignores that each SPARK attempt uses three role-specific LLM calls, whereas the baseline may use one. Wall-clock time, token usage, LLM calls, failed proposals, and training cost should all be reported under matched budgets.

The statistical evidence is inadequate for the headline accuracy claims. Tables 1 and 2 contain single values without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or training-seed counts; the baseline comparisons and ablations are not reported across repeated searches. Selecting the best architecture through stochastic search and then reporting one training outcome risks winner's-curse and seed-selection effects.

The only five-seed result, Figure A.1, appears incompatible with the main result: its best-so-far OOD curves saturate near 0.22-0.25, whereas the text and Figure 2 claim 0.8374 on DFS. The manuscript does not explain a different metric, task, or normalization. This directly undermines the claimed robustness across seeds.

The controlled comparison is underspecified. It is unclear whether OpenEvolve and the other reimplemented baselines receive identical feasibility filtering, editable regions, archive settings, context, and total LLM-call/token budgets. Lower SPARK entanglement is also partly tautological because SPARK explicitly rejects edits outside the selected region; it does not by itself establish that factor selection, rather than hard filtering or extra LLM calls, causes the accuracy gain. A matched baseline with the same filters and call budget but random/fixed factor routing is needed.

Presentation contains material inconsistencies: the main text says the supplement covers all 18 CLRS tasks, the conclusion reports wins on 12/18 and 10/18, but Table A.1 contains 30 tasks. The main table reports only a favorable 10-task subset without a stated preselection rule. The full table reveals severe negative transfer on tasks such as BFS (100.0 for EP versus 70.6 for SPARK) and Floyd-Warshall (61.4 versus 32.9), which warrants analysis and tempers the broad generalization claim.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The paper does not provide complete role prompts, sanitization rules, router retry count, migration period, archive discretization, training hyperparameters, random seeds, API snapshot/configuration, hardware, token and monetary costs, or a code-release location. Referring to default OpenEvolve settings and printing selected evolved functions is not enough to reproduce the search.

Originality is moderate rather than high: decomposing code into tagged regions, routing an edit to one region, and rejecting nonlocal changes is a natural application of established structure-aware editing and constrained program search. The paper would need stronger controlled evidence to establish that its particular Operator/Action factorization yields a general NAS insight rather than a CLRS-specific engineering heuristic. Overall, the idea is promising and the reported numbers are encouraging, but the unresolved accounting contradictions and missing statistical controls prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and practically relevant failure mode in LLM-based code-level NAS: a rewrite can simultaneously alter operators, wiring, and interfaces, making iterative changes difficult to attribute and frequently invalid.

SPARK is conceptually straightforward and clearly specified through scope routing, directive generation, scoped refinement, region tags, and inexpensive syntax/interface/shape checks. The algorithms and illustrative evolution trace make the intended workflow understandable.

The evaluation is broader than a single headline result: it includes all 30 CLRS tasks, two LLM editors, component and scope-control ablations, search trajectories, executability measurements, model MACs, and five non-CLRS benchmarks. The reported full-suite arithmetic is internally consistent: 83.91% average accuracy and improvements over the CLRS and EvoPrompting entries on 21/30 and 19/30 tasks, respectively.
The scope-control ablation is useful: random or fixed region selection is substantially worse than ASR+SAR and full SPARK, suggesting that the result is not explained solely by inserting region tags.

Presentation is generally clear and the paper honestly acknowledges imperfect cross-task transfer, extra LLM calls, and reliance on manually defined factors. The societal-risk discussion is brief but proportionate to this primarily methodological work.
weaknesses: The central evaluation appears to adaptively optimize on the metric later reported as OOD test accuracy. Section 4.2 says search performance is measured using the CLRS OOD split, the archive descriptor explicitly includes `ood_acc`, and the best architecture is selected from repeated evaluations on that signal. Unless this is a separate validation-OOD set—which is never stated—57–100 adaptive queries contaminate the DFS test result. Similar validation-versus-test separation is not specified for the additional benchmarks. This is a major soundness problem.

The claimed 28.1x efficiency gain is not a controlled speedup measurement. It divides EvoPrompting's stated 1600 evaluations by the iteration at which one SPARK run attains its best result (57), despite different search procedures, feedback protocols, proposal validity, and LLM-call costs. SPARK uses up to three role-specific calls per proposal and excludes rejected proposals from its evaluation count. No matched target-performance curve, total LLM calls, GPU-hours, or uncertainty supports the 28.1x claim.

The comparison protocol is internally ambiguous. Section 4 says EvoPrompting evolves across multiple tasks, whereas Section 4.2 says each method searches on DFS and transfers the incumbent to the other tasks. It is consequently unclear whether the EP entries are from the published task-specific procedure or a reimplementation under DFS transfer. This ambiguity undermines the main 10-task and 30-task comparisons.

Statistical evidence is inadequate for a stochastic and selection-heavy pipeline. Most tables report a single number without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the 28.1x claim is explicitly based on 'that run.' Although one appendix trajectory shows five SPARK seeds, no corresponding baseline seed distribution is supplied, and it is unclear which seeds produced the tabulated results. Large ablation differences and modest non-CLRS gains therefore cannot be distinguished from search/training variance.

The entanglement evidence is partly tautological. SPARK explicitly permits changes only inside one selected region and rejects non-local edits, while entanglement is defined as changing multiple regions or frozen scaffolding. A lower measured entanglement rate therefore follows mechanically from the constraint. The proposed causal chain from lower entanglement to validity and accuracy is not isolated from feasibility filtering, extra LLM calls, or prompt/context differences, and the p_v^k argument assumes independence without empirical validation.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract's code-availability URL is blank. The role prompts, sanitization rules, exact region definitions for every benchmark, training hyperparameters, dataset splits, random seeds, API/model configuration beyond temperature, OpenEvolve settings hidden behind 'defaults,' and complete per-run results are not provided. DeepSeek-R1 is accessed through an unspecified API endpoint, further limiting replication.

The non-CLRS experiments are too underspecified to establish broad generality. The manuscript does not explain how OPERATOR/ACTION regions were constructed for each task, what objective split drove search, or whether hyperparameters and factor definitions were chosen after observing results. Several comparisons also use 100 proposals for SPARK versus 400 for EoH/FunSearch while omitting uncertainty, making the results difficult to interpret.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than high: the main mechanism is a manually designed two-region edit constraint plus role-specific prompting and validity checks, closely related to established structured editing and mutation-operator ideas. The term 'progressive knowledge activation' overstates what is demonstrated; there is no direct measurement of activated knowledge, only routing and constrained generation.

The limitations section does not discuss the most consequential threats—possible test-set reuse, unmatched search cost, missing uncertainty, dependence on proprietary/API-served LLM behavior, and manual benchmark-specific scope construction. For the medical-diagnosis benchmark, the paper should also clarify that this small benchmark does not support clinical applicability, although no immediate material ethical violation is evident.

strengths: Soundness: The core design is understandable and implementable in principle: SPARK separates scope selection, directive generation, and scoped refinement, then applies syntax, interface, shape, and masking checks before expensive evaluation.

Empirical scope: The paper reports a full 30-task CLRS comparison, a DFS-to-other-tasks transfer experiment, five non-CLRS benchmarks, search trajectories, and several component and scope-control ablations. This is broader than a single-task proof of concept.

Significance and originality: Constraining LLM architecture edits to explicit functional regions is a sensible, potentially useful response to unreliable free-form code mutation. The framing of cross-region edits as functional entanglement provides an intuitive diagnostic, although the underlying mechanism is incremental rather than fundamentally new.

Presentation and limitations: The main algorithm and Operator/Action factorization are explained clearly, and the paper honestly acknowledges imperfect task transfer, extra LLM-call cost, and dependence on manually defined regions. The impact statement raises no unresolved material ethical concern for the presented research. weaknesses: Soundness: The headline 28.1x efficiency claim is not supported by comparable accounting. It divides EvoPrompting's 1600 evaluations by SPARK's reported 57 evaluated candidates despite describing different search protocols (multi-task evolution versus DFS-only search and transfer), and it ignores SPARK's three role-specific LLM calls and rejected proposals. More seriously, the claim that proposal attempt 57 corresponds to 57 evaluated candidates conflicts with Figure 2c, where SPARK's cumulative valid rate near that point is only roughly 0.5–0.6. Under the paper's own one-proposal/one-candidate definition, these quantities cannot both be correct.

Soundness: The causal story is insufficiently established. SPARK defines non-factor-local proposals as infeasible and rejects them, so its lower measured entanglement rate follows partly by construction. The results do not cleanly separate the benefits of routing and directives from those of rejection/filtering, added LLM calls, or other implementation differences. The argument that editing k scopes gives feasibility approximately p_v^k assumes independence without evidence and should be treated only as intuition.

Statistical evidence: Nearly every headline table reports one number per method without standard deviations, confidence intervals, seed-level outcomes, or significance tests. Five SPARK seeds appear only in Appendix Figure A.1; corresponding multi-seed baseline distributions are absent. Best-of-search results are especially vulnerable to search and training variance, so the large claimed gains cannot be judged reliably. Figure A.1 is also unexplainedly scaled around 0–0.25 for 'best-so-far OOD accuracy,' inconsistent with the reported DFS value of 0.8374.

Baseline fairness: The protocol description is internally inconsistent. Section 4.2 says each method receives the same DFS-based 100-attempt search-and-transfer protocol, while elsewhere EvoPrompting is described as evolving across multiple tasks and using 1600 evaluations. It is unclear which baseline values were newly reproduced, which were imported, and whether editor model, prompts, feasibility handling, selection rules, and training randomness were matched. The additional benchmarks also compare 100-candidate methods against 400-candidate methods without a budget-normalized analysis.

Reproducibility: The abstract's code URL is blank. The exact route, directive, and edit prompts are not provided, despite prompts being central to the method. Important details are missing or deferred to unspecified defaults, including seeds, training hyperparameters, archive discretization, migration period, router retries, cascade behavior, API settings beyond temperature, benchmark-specific factor definitions, and complete cost accounting. A changing hosted DeepSeek endpoint further increases the need for saved outputs and exact configurations.

Significance and generality: The method relies on manually marking two disjoint code regions in one CLRS module. The non-CLRS experiments do not explain how Operator and Action regions were defined, how much human work was required, or whether the same rules and prompts were used. Consequently, broad claims that factor-conditioned editing transfers across diverse interfaces are not adequately demonstrated.

Originality: Region-restricted code editing, explicit mutation scopes, validation checks, and staged LLM prompting are individually established ideas. The paper's combination may be useful, but the conceptual advance is modest, and the term 'knowledge activation' overstates what is operationally a manually scoped prompting and filtering procedure.

Presentation: Several statements create avoidable ambiguity, including claiming a 'single prompt template' while defining three role-specific prompts and attributing a small fixed model-level MAC overhead to the 'SPARK editing interface,' even though SPARK is a search-time procedure. The unusually large non-CLRS gains, such as MNIST-1D average accuracy increasing from 70.25 to 95.99, receive too little protocol detail or variance analysis to be credible as presented. These evidential and reproducibility problems outweigh the promising idea and warrant rejection in the current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: SPARK offers an intuitive structure-aware alternative to unconstrained LLM code rewriting. Explicitly separating OPERATOR and ACTION edits, routing each revision to one region, and enforcing locality is a useful design pattern for LLM-driven NAS.

Soundness: The feasibility pipeline is sensibly designed: syntax, interface, tensor-shape, masking, and region-locality checks reject invalid proposals before expensive training. The distinction between proposal attempts and trained candidates is also clearly stated.

Evidence: The manuscript reports substantial empirical gains, including 83.91% mean accuracy across all 30 CLRS tasks, and it discloses notable transfer failures on BFS, Floyd-Warshall, and KMP rather than showing only favorable tasks.

Ablations: The comparisons against global rewriting, random or fixed scopes, ASR without RC, and RC+SAR with random routing help separate the effects of region tags, routing, and refinement. Results with both DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus provide limited evidence of editor robustness.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithms, factor-local feasible set, and scope-control experiments are generally clear. Figures and tables are legible, and the appendix includes examples of evolved programs and an illustrative SPARK step.

Limitations/ethics: The paper honestly acknowledges manual factor design, imperfect cross-task transfer, and extra LLM calls. The societal-impact discussion is proportionate to the largely methodological contribution, with no evident unresolved ethical issue.
weaknesses: Soundness: The search objective appears to use CLRS OOD accuracy directly: Section 4.2 says evolution is measured using the OOD split, and the selected incumbent is then reported using OOD accuracy. If this is the benchmark test split, architecture selection has leaked test information into the final evaluation, invalidating the central performance comparison. The manuscript does not identify a separate validation split or a final untouched test evaluation.

Soundness: Most headline tables provide only single point estimates, without means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Although one appendix trajectory is said to aggregate five seeds, the main 83.74% DFS result, 30-task transfer table, ablations, and non-CLRS results do not report seed-level variability. Best-so-far selection makes this omission especially consequential.

The claimed 28.1x efficiency improvement is not a controlled speedup. It divides EvoPrompting's 1600 evaluations by the iteration at which one SPARK run found its best candidate, despite acknowledged differences in search protocol, task coverage, backbone, editor, and proposal validity. It also ignores SPARK's three role-specific LLM calls per proposal, invalid proposals, wall time, and GPU cost. At most, this is a narrow evaluated-candidate ratio under incompatible settings.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently established. EvoPrompting searches across multiple tasks whereas SPARK searches only DFS and transfers one architecture; it is unclear which baseline numbers were rerun under the identical editor, prompts, seeds, and transfer protocol. FunSearch and EoH are adapted from algorithm search, but implementation details needed to judge whether those adaptations are competitive are absent.

The causal claim that reduced functional entanglement produces better search is only partly supported. SPARK enforces locality by construction, so its lower measured entanglement is largely tautological; the feasibility checker and extra routing/directive calls are bundled with the proposed factorization. The reported ablations do not match total LLM-call or wall-clock budgets and therefore cannot isolate the mechanism cleanly.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract's code link is blank, and the paper omits the actual prompts, complete region templates, exact OpenEvolve configuration, training hyperparameters, dataset splits, random seeds, API/model-serving details, and per-method LLM-call totals. Referring to defaults is fragile, particularly for a rapidly changing external codebase and black-box API model.

The non-CLRS evidence is under-specified and statistically weak. The manuscript does not explain how OPERATOR/ACTION regions are defined for each heterogeneous benchmark, whether validation or test performance guides search, or how splits and repeated runs are handled. Some methods receive 400 proposals while others receive 100, and no uncertainty is reported; thus these experiments do not convincingly establish broad generality.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the core mechanism combines manually tagged code regions, an LLM router, directive generation, and standard feasibility checks. The paper distinguishes this from grammar-constrained editing, but does not demonstrate that the proposed formulation yields a general principle beyond this hand-designed two-region decomposition.

Presentation contains potentially misleading statements. Table 1 describes a fixed MAC overhead introduced by the 'SPARK editing interface,' even though a search-time editing interface should not itself affect inference-time architecture MACs. The paper also alternates between a fixed evaluation budget and a fixed proposal-attempt budget, making efficiency comparisons difficult to interpret.

The limitations section omits the most consequential risks: possible OOD/test-set selection, lack of statistical uncertainty, dependence on a proprietary or externally served LLM, and the incompatibility of the headline efficiency comparison. These issues prevent the current evidence from reliably supporting the central empirical claims.
